nameStory: The bigeye scad gets its name from its most striking feature – unusually large, prominent eyes that seem almost too big for its sleek body. These oversized peepers help this oceanic fish spot tiny prey and predators in the vast blue waters where it spends its life.
description: The bigeye scad is a streamlined, silvery fish that's built for speed in open ocean waters. With its torpedo-shaped body and distinctive large eyes, it's unmistakably a member of the jack family. These fish typically grow to about a foot long and travel in schools, making them more likely to be spotted in groups rather than alone when they venture into New England waters.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Exceptionally large, round eyes that appear almost goggle-like – much larger than you'd expect for the fish's body size, giving it a perpetually surprised expression

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Sleek, torpedo-shaped body that feels firm and muscular to the touch, built like a living missile for cutting through water

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright silvery sides that flash like mirrors in sunlight, with a blue-green back that helps it blend with ocean depths when viewed from above

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Sharp-edged dorsal and anal fins set far back on the body, with a deeply forked tail that feels stiff and powerful – classic jack family features

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, terminal mouth positioned at the tip of the snout, designed for picking off small prey rather than gulping large meals

habitat: Bigeye scads are true ocean wanderers, occasionally showing up in New England's offshore waters during warmer months. They prefer the open Atlantic beyond the continental shelf, but may venture closer to shore when following schools of small fish or when carried by warm currents. Look for them in deep, clear waters rather than near shore or in estuaries.

seasonality.spring: Rare visitors may begin appearing in offshore New England waters as ocean temperatures start to warm, usually staying in deeper waters beyond typical recreational fishing zones.
seasonality.summer: Most likely time to encounter bigeye scads in New England waters, when warm currents and abundant prey may draw them north from their typical tropical haunts.
seasonality.fall: Any remaining individuals typically move back toward warmer southern waters as ocean temperatures begin to drop.
seasonality.winter: Extremely rare in New England waters during winter months, as these tropical fish seek warmer waters far to the south.

funFact: Bigeye scads are such strong swimmers that they can leap completely out of the water when escaping predators, and their huge eyes can actually detect polarized light patterns in water that are completely invisible to human eyes!
confusionNotes: With only 6 recorded observations in New England, bigeye scads are most likely to be confused with other jack family members like Atlantic mackerel or small bluefish. The key difference is those enormous eyes – no other fish in our waters has eyes quite that dramatically oversized for its body.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'scad,' bigeye scads aren't closely related to the herring family fish we typically call scads in New England waters. This is a naming confusion that arose from their similar schooling behavior and commercial fishing importance in different parts of the world.
compareHints: Since bigeye scad is the only member of its genus in our dataset, compare it to other jacks like pompano or amberjack. Bigeye scads are much smaller and more delicately built than most jacks, with that distinctive large-eyed appearance. Unlike the deeper-bodied pompanos or the robust amberjacks, bigeye scads maintain a more torpedo-like profile throughout their lives.
